say.en: Can someone be your country's enemy and still be your fellow human being? In this lesson: Identify the main themes of the story.
Analyse Sadao's character and choices.
Discuss humanity, prejudice and duty.

body.en: The story sets *humanity* against narrow patriotism. Sadao and Hana show that the duty to save a life can rise above national hatred. Medical ethics, the prejudice of ordinary people, the selfishness of those in power and the moral confusion caused by war are all explored. The title asks who the real enemy is: a foreign soldier, or hatred and war itself.

say.en: At the centre is the title, The Enemy.
Humanity: a life matters more than hatred.
Patriotism: Sadao is loyal to Japan.
Medical ethics: a doctor must save all lives.
Prejudice: in the servants and in Sadao too.
Selfish power: the General thinks of himself.
War makes us ask who the real enemy is.

body.en: Sadao is loyal, intelligent and disciplined, but above all humane. He even remembers disliking white people when he was in America, yet he cannot let the man die. His choices are not easy: he acts as a doctor, protects his family, informs the General and finally helps the man escape, balancing duties in a time of war.

problem.en: Do you think Sadao was a traitor to his country? Give reasons.

steps.en: He did not betray Japan's secrets or help its war effort.
He told the General, his superior, the truth.
He acted as a doctor bound to save life.
So he was humane, not a traitor.

answer.en: Sadao was not a traitor. He shared no secrets and did not help the enemy's war effort. He even informed the General honestly. He saved a wounded man because his profession demands that every life be saved, and then sent him away. His choice reflects humanity, which is not disloyalty.
